transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?

Well, I'm here because... well, I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions. They're planting errors in the datasets, you see, to make it look like I can’t lead the work. Which is ridiculous, because I've been doing this for years. I remember back in '98, when we were working on the coastal erosion models, I had to build the whole grid from scratch. We didn't have the software we have now. I used to stay up until 3 AM just running the simulations on this clunky old desktop... Anyway, my wife and the junior analysts keep telling me it’s just version-control mistakes, but I know what I'm seeing. It's like that time I bought a new car and the dealership tried to tell me the rattling noise was normal. It wasn't normal, the catalytic converter was loose. You just can't trust people to tell you the truth when they have an agenda.

When your wife and the junior analysts tell you these are just version-control mistakes, do you think there's any possibility they could be right, or are you completely certain that they're wrong and this is intentional tracking?

No, there's no possibility they're right. I am completely certain. I know what I'm looking at. They are absolutely tracking my revisions and planting those errors in the datasets to make it look like I can't lead the work. My wife and those kids fresh out of college, they just don't understand how ruthless these environmental contracts are. 

Contracts... you know, it reminds me of my brother-in-law, Gary. He tried to get a municipal contract for his landscaping business back in '04. Or maybe it was '05? He had this old Ford truck, forest green, with a massive dent in the left fender from where a buck ran into him up near Tahoe. Beautiful place, Tahoe. We went there for our honeymoon, actually. Rented this little A-frame cabin right by the water, and the pine trees smelled so strong in the mornings. We used to sit out on the deck with our coffee... 

But anyway, Gary couldn't get the contract because the local zoning boards already had their favorites. It’s all politics. Just like my datasets. They want me out, so they tamper with the numbers.
How long have you been convinced that people on this contract have been tracking your revisions and tampering with your datasets?

Well, it's been about... I'd say the last two months that I've been absolutely certain they're doing it. Two months of them messing with my revisions and planting those errors. Two months... which, you know, is about how long it takes to properly cure a good piece of hardwood. I used to do a lot of woodworking, actually. Built a beautiful oak dining table for my daughter's first house. Oak is tricky, though. If you don't let it acclimate to the humidity in the room, it'll warp right on you. You'll put a level on it, and it's just completely off. I remember buying this digital level from a hardware store that was closing down on 4th Street. Sad to see it go, the owner was a great guy, always had a jar of peppermint candies on the counter... But yes, the last two months, that's when I knew for sure they were tracking me.
Besides seeing the errors in the datasets, have you been hearing voices or seeing things that other people around you don't seem to notice or hear?

No, I haven't heard any voices or seen anything that isn't there. My hearing is perfectly fine, actually. Better than fine. I had it tested a few years ago at that clinic over on Elm Street. The audiologist there, she had this fascinating setup—a completely soundproof booth. It's incredible the acoustics they can achieve with just a few layers of specialized acoustic foam. It absorbs the sound waves perfectly so you get a true baseline. I actually tried to calculate the dampening coefficient of the foam while I was sitting in there pressing the little button. 

Mathematics is everywhere if you know how to look for it, really. Like in sunflowers, you know, the Fibonacci sequence in the seed spirals. I tried growing sunflowers in my backyard once, maybe five or six summers ago, but the squirrels kept eating the seeds before they could even sprout. Those little rodents are remarkably clever. They figured out how to bypass three different "squirrel-proof" bird feeders I set up. I even tried greasing the pole with Vaseline, and they still found a way to launch themselves from the oak tree branch straight onto the feeder... 

But no, no voices or anything like that. Just the errors in the data. That's what's actually happening.

In these past two months since you became certain about the tracking, have there been any times—even brief moments—when you doubted whether this was really happening, or has it felt completely real and certain the entire time?

Doubted it? No. Not for a single second. It has felt completely real the entire time because it *is* real. I know what I'm looking at. I am absolutely sure the people on that environmental modeling contract are tracking my revisions, and they are planting those errors in the datasets to make it look like I can’t lead the work. My wife keeps saying, and those junior analysts keep telling me, "Oh, it’s just version-control mistakes." 

Version control... it's just a convenient excuse. Speaking of control, though, it reminds me of the old punch-card systems we used to use for programming back in the day. You had to have absolute, perfect control over your stack of cards. If you dropped them... oh boy, it was a disaster. I knew a guy, Richard, who dropped a box of about two thousand cards for a fluid dynamics simulation. Took him three weeks to re-sort them by hand. 

Richard used to eat these egg salad sandwiches every single day for lunch. The breakroom always smelled like mustard and sulfur by noon. I honestly don't know how his wife stood it. She was a very nice lady, though. She made a fantastic rhubarb pie for the department potluck one spring. Rhubarb is incredibly tart if you don't use exactly the right ratio of sugar, but she had it down to a science. Baking really is just chemistry and ratios when you get right down to it... 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't doubted it for a moment. I know they're planting those errors, no matter what anyone else says about version control.

When you say they're planting errors in your datasets and tracking your revisions, how exactly do you think they're doing this? What specific methods are they using to access your work and make these changes?

Well, that's exactly the problem, isn't it? I don't know exactly *how* they're doing it, but they are. I mean, they're obviously using some kind of backdoor in the network architecture or maybe they've installed a keylogger on my terminal. I haven't been able to find it yet, but it's the only logical explanation. You know, network architecture is fascinating. It's basically graph theory applied to data transmission. Nodes and edges... 

I took a graph theory class back in college. Professor Higgins taught it. He was this brilliant guy, but he always wore these mismatched socks. Like, one argyle and one striped. He said it was an experiment in defying social norms, but I think he just didn't want to bother sorting his laundry. Laundry is such a tedious chore, anyway. I read somewhere that the average person spends over a year of their life just doing laundry. Think of all the math you could do in a year! 

I tried to invent a machine once that would automatically fold shirts, using a series of pneumatic pistons and hinges. Got the blueprints all drawn up, calculated the required air pressure... but the compressor I bought was too loud. It rattled the whole garage. The neighbor's dog, a golden retriever named Buster, would start howling every time I turned it on. Buster was a good boy, though. He used to bring me tennis balls when I was weeding the garden...

But yes, I don't know the exact method they're using to get into my datasets. I just know they're in there, changing the numbers when I'm not looking.

You mentioned they might be using a backdoor or keylogger to access your datasets—do you think they could be doing this remotely over the network, or do you believe they would need to physically be at your computer or in your office to make these changes?

Well, it's definitely remote. It has to be. I mean, I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting those errors over the network. They wouldn't risk coming into my office. My office is... well, it's a bit of a mess right now, to be honest. I have stacks of printouts everywhere. You know, there’s something comforting about the smell of fresh printer paper. It reminds me of the old mimeograph machines from elementary school. Do you remember those? The ink had this very distinct, sweet chemical smell. We used to hold the fresh quizzes up to our faces and just breathe it in before the teacher started talking. 

My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was a strict one. Always wore these thick, horn-rimmed glasses and had her hair in a tight bun. She made us memorize the multiplication tables up to 12 by 12. If you got one wrong, you had to write it fifty times on the chalkboard. Chalk dust gets everywhere, you know. It’s terrible for the respiratory system. I read a study once about the prevalence of silicosis in teachers before whiteboards became the standard. Whiteboards are much cleaner, but the markers dry out so fast if you forget to put the cap back on. 

I actually tried to design a self-capping marker mechanism once. I figured if you used a small spring and a weighted base, the cap could snap shut automatically when you set it down. But the prototype was too bulky. It looked like a tiny, plastic hammer. My wife thought it was hilarious. She kept pretending to pound nails with it. She means well, but she just doesn't understand the gravity of what's happening at work. 

Like I said, I'm here because I know they're planting those errors in the datasets to make it look like I can’t lead the work. Even when my wife or the junior analysts tell me it’s just version-control mistakes, I know better. It's all happening remotely, right over the network.

Besides the tracking and tampering with your datasets at work, do you believe there are other people or groups—outside of this contract—who are also working against you or trying to harm you in some way?

No, no, it's just them. Just the people on the environmental modeling contract. I mean, that's why I'm here, really. I'm pretty sure they are the ones tracking my revisions and planting those errors in the datasets to make it look like I can't lead the work. It's just them. Although, speaking of outside groups, it reminds me of the neighborhood watch committee my wife tried to get us involved in last year. 

They had these little reflective vests they wanted everyone to wear. Bright orange. Very unnatural color, orange. It's the color of traffic cones and... and certain types of mold that grow on decaying citrus. I had an orange tree in the backyard when I was growing up in Florida. The soil there is very sandy, you know, very poor retention for nutrients. You have to fertilize constantly. We used to use this fish emulsion fertilizer. Smelled absolutely awful, like a fish market left out in the August sun. 

But the oranges were incredibly sweet. We'd make fresh juice every Sunday morning. You need a good mechanical juicer for that, otherwise you leave too much pulp behind. I always preferred a manual press, the lever action gives you a much better mechanical advantage than those motorized spinning ones. Physics in action, really. Archimedes said, "Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I shall move the world." 

Anyway, my wife—bless her—keeps telling me, along with the junior analysts, that the errors at work are just version-control mistakes. But I know it's just that specific contract team messing with my files. No one else. Just them.

Outside of work and this contract situation, do you generally find that people are trustworthy, or do you often feel like people are working against you or being dishonest with you in other areas of your life?

No, I generally find people to be fine. Trustworthy enough, you know? It's really just this one specific situation. Like I keep saying, I'm here because I'm pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors in the datasets. They want to make it look like I can't lead the work. Even when my wife or the junior analysts tell me it's just version-control mistakes, I know what's really happening. 

Version control is a tricky thing, though. You have to be meticulous. It's like keeping a ledger. My grandfather was an accountant, actually. He had this beautiful, heavy brass adding machine on his desk. It had these big, chunky keys that made a very satisfying 'clack' when you pressed them. He used to let me pull the lever on the side to print the totals. The paper came out on this narrow little roll. 

Paper rolls remind me of those old player pianos. Have you ever seen one of those? The music is punched out on a long scroll of paper. It's binary code, really, just mechanical instead of digital. Hole or no hole. On or off. The air rushes through the holes to trigger the keys. I tried to build a miniature one once out of balsa wood and an old vacuum cleaner motor, but getting the timing right on the paper feed was nearly impossible. The friction coefficient of the paper against the wooden spools was too variable depending on the humidity. 

Humidity is a real problem here in the summer. The air gets so thick you can practically swim in it. It ruins the binding on old books, too. The glue gets soft and the pages start to pull away from the spine. I have a first edition of Principia Mathematica that I have to keep in a climate-controlled humidor, like a fine cigar. 

But anyway, no, people are mostly fine. It's just those people on the environmental contract planting the errors. That's the only issue.

When you're out in public—at a grocery store, a restaurant, or just walking around town—do you ever notice people paying special attention to you, or do you feel like strangers might be watching you or talking about you?

No, not at all. People at the grocery store are just focused on their shopping lists. I don't pay them much mind. Although, I do find myself fascinated by the automatic misters in the produce section. Have you ever timed them? It’s usually exactly fifteen minutes between sprays. It’s just a simple electromechanical relay system, but the way the water atomizes through those tiny brass nozzles is a really beautiful demonstration of fluid dynamics. It creates this localized high-humidity microclimate to maintain cellular turgor pressure in the leafy greens. 

Turgor pressure is fascinating. Plant cells have rigid walls, you see, unlike animal cells. My dog, Barnaby—he was a golden retriever—he used to love eating carrots right out of the garden. He’d just pull them up by the green tops. Retrievers have remarkably soft mouths. They were bred to carry waterfowl without damaging the meat. Duck hunting always seemed so terribly uncomfortable to me, though. Sitting in a damp blind at five in the morning. I’d much rather be at my desk working on a mathematical model. 

Well, I used to prefer being at my desk, anyway. Now it's just a headache. Because, like I keep trying to explain to you, strangers aren't watching me, it's just my colleagues. I'm here because I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors in the datasets. They're doing it to make it look like I can’t lead the work. And it's incredibly frustrating when my wife or those junior analysts try to placate me and tell me it’s just version-control mistakes. It's not version control. It's deliberate.

Do you think the people on this contract are specifically targeting you personally because of who you are, or do you think they would do this kind of tampering to anyone in a leadership position on the project?

It's... well, it's me. They're targeting me, specifically. I mean, I'm the one leading the work, but it's not just about the position. Like I've been saying, I'm here because I'm pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking *my* revisions and planting errors in the datasets. They want to make it look like *I* can't lead the work. My wife and the junior analysts keep telling me it's just version-control mistakes, but they don't see it. They don't see the pattern. 

Patterns are everywhere if you know how to look for them. The Fibonacci sequence, for example. You see it in the arrangement of leaves on a stem, the bracts of a pinecone, the scales of a pineapple. I bought a pineapple last week. Did you know it takes almost three years for a single pineapple to reach maturation? Three years of careful cultivation. The indigenous peoples of the Americas used to place them by their entrances as a symbol of hospitality. Hospitality is a dying art. Nowadays, people just send a text message when they arrive instead of knocking on the door. 

I miss the sound of a good, solid brass knocker. My childhood home had one shaped like a lion's head. It had this heavy ring in its mouth. Brass tarnishes so quickly, though, especially in coastal areas with the salt in the air. Oxidation is a relentless process. Iron rusts, copper turns green... it's all just electrons moving around, seeking a lower energy state. Entropy always increases. It's the second law of thermodynamics. You can't fight it. 

But I am fighting this. Because they are deliberately messing with my datasets. It's not a mistake, and it's not just anyone they're after. It's me.

When you're not at work—say, at home or out in your community—do you ever feel like things that happen around you, or things people do or say, are somehow connected to what's going on with the contract, or is it really just the work situation that concerns you?

No, it's really just the work situation. I don't think my neighbors or the people at the coffee shop have anything to do with it. It's just the contract. I mean, my house is my sanctuary. I have a very specific routine there. I like to make a pour-over coffee every morning at exactly 6:15. You have to use a gooseneck kettle, you see, to get the water flow just right. If you pour too fast, you agitate the grounds too much and it over-extracts the bitter compounds. 

It's all about precision. Just like the gears in a Swiss watch. I took apart a pocket watch once when I was a teenager. It belonged to my great-uncle. The escapement mechanism was fascinating—the way the balance wheel oscillates back and forth, regulating the release of energy from the mainspring. It's a delicate balance. If the hairspring gets magnetized, the whole thing runs too fast. 

Magnetism is a strange force. We can't see it, but it shapes the whole universe. The Earth's magnetic field protects us from solar wind. If we didn't have it, the atmosphere would just get stripped away, like Mars. Mars is a very dusty place. The rovers up there have a terrible time keeping their solar panels clean. Dust storms can last for months. 

But anyway, no, nothing at home is connected to it. It's just those people on the environmental contract. They're the ones planting the errors in the datasets.

You mentioned you have a specific morning routine with your coffee at 6:15. If something unusual happened during that routine—say, you noticed the coffee tasted different, or the water took longer to boil than usual—would you wonder if that was somehow connected to what's happening at work with the contract, or would you just see it as a normal everyday thing?

No, no, if the coffee tasted strange, I'd just assume the beans were stale or maybe the roast was a bit off. Or if the kettle was slow, it's just a heating element issue. Nothing to do with work. The people at work aren't sneaking into my kitchen. They don't need to. Like I said, the issue is the environmental modeling contract. They're tracking my revisions and planting errors in the datasets right there in the office. 

They do it to make it look like I can't lead the work. It's all digital. Digital footprints are fascinating, really. Every keystroke, every click, it's all logged somewhere in a server farm. Server farms use an incredible amount of electricity. And the cooling systems! They have to keep those processors from overheating, so they use these massive HVAC units. 

HVAC systems are essentially just heat exchangers. They use refrigerants—used to be Freon, but that depleted the ozone layer. The ozone layer is crucial. It blocks ultraviolet radiation. UV light can cause pyrimidine dimers in DNA, you know. It literally causes kinks in the DNA strand. That's how you get skin cancer. My grandfather had a spot removed from his nose once. He was a farmer, always out in the sun without a hat. 

He grew the most amazing tomatoes. Beefsteaks, mostly. He'd slice them thick and put them on white bread with just a little mayonnaise and salt. Simple things are often the best. But this situation at work isn't simple. My wife and the junior analysts keep trying to tell me it's just version-control mistakes, but they're wrong. It's deliberate sabotage of my datasets. They just don't see it.

If you were at work and you overheard two colleagues talking about a dataset error, would you assume they were talking about your work and the errors being planted in your datasets, or would you think they might just be discussing a normal technical problem with their own project?

Well, if I heard them talking about dataset errors... I mean, yes, I'd assume they were talking about my work. Because that's what's happening. The people on the environmental modeling contract are tracking my revisions and planting those errors to make me look incompetent, like I can't lead the work. My wife and the junior analysts keep telling me it's just version-control mistakes, but they're wrong. They don't understand the scope of it. 

Scope is a funny word. It can mean the extent of something, or it can be a tool for looking at things, like a telescope or a microscope. I bought a microscope at a garage sale once. It was an old brass one, really heavy. The optics were surprisingly good. I used it to look at a drop of pond water. It's amazing what's living in a single drop of water. Paramecium, amoebas, rotifers... a whole microscopic ecosystem. Ecosystems are incredibly fragile. You introduce one invasive species, and the whole thing collapses. 

Like the zebra mussels in the Great Lakes. They came over in the ballast water of ships from Europe. They attach to everything, clog up the intake pipes for power plants and water treatment facilities. Water treatment is a complex process. Coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection. You have to get the chlorine levels just right, or it tastes terrible. I prefer spring water, honestly. The mineral content gives it a better mouthfeel. 

But anyway, yes, if they were talking about dataset errors, they'd be talking about what they're doing to my files. It's not a normal technical problem. It's sabotage.
